idiom_name: indirect enum + switch, operations as functions or computed properties
implementation_notes: Swift's recursive enums give the pattern's structure natively: model the node set as an enum (indirect where it is recursive) and write each operation as a function with an exhaustive switch, so the compiler refuses to compile once a case is added and the operation is never forced into the node type. The GoF double dispatch is subsumed by matching on the case, and `default` is unnecessary (and undesirable) over an enum because the switch must cover every case. Where the hierarchy is a class hierarchy that third parties extend, or belongs to a framework, Swift keeps the protocol-visitor form - and SwiftSyntax is exactly that, shipping SyntaxVisitor/SyntaxAnyVisitor with per-node visit hooks and a continue/skip return value.
pitfalls: A default case over your own enum silently swallows new cases; omit it so the compiler enforces coverage.
Recursive cases require indirection and deep trees can still overflow the stack during recursion - iterative walks or an explicit work queue are needed for untrusted input.
Enums cannot be extended by clients, so a DSL that third parties must extend needs the protocol/visitor form instead.
Swift enums with associated values are value types: visitors that mutate the tree must return a new value (or use a class-based model) rather than editing in place.

variants.name: Protocol visitor over a framework hierarchy (SwiftSyntax)
variants.idiom_name: SwiftSyntax SyntaxVisitor / SyntaxAnyVisitor with visit(_:) hooks
variants.implementation_notes: When the node hierarchy belongs to a framework, Swift ships the classic visitor: subclass SyntaxVisitor and override visit(_: SomeSyntax) with a SyntaxVisitorContinueKind result to control descent, or use SyntaxAnyVisitor for a single visitAny hook, and SyntaxRewriter for transformations. That is the pattern's role structure in library form, complete with the classic trade: the node kinds are the framework's, and default implementations mean an unhandled case is silently passed to the default hook, so coverage is a code-review property rather than a compiler one. Use it for macros, linters and formatters that must work over Swift source they do not own.
pitfalls: Returning .skipChildren prunes the subtree silently; a visitor that accumulates results and forgets to descend reports partial answers.
The viewMode must be chosen deliberately (sourceAccurate vs fixedUp); the two produce different trees and therefore different visit sequences.
SyntaxVisitor visits nodes only - tokens and trivia need SyntaxAnyVisitor or explicit token hooks, and mixing the two changes what the operation sees.
SwiftSyntax trees are large value types; copying nodes in a visitor is expensive, so walk in place and collect ids or small values instead.
